text: Course 3's Chapter 3 covered building catalog items, categories, and variables, but none of that work makes a request actually do anything on its own. Older ServiceNow implementations wired fulfillment logic directly to the legacy Workflow editor, attached to the catalog item itself. Flow Designer replaces that path entirely: fulfillment logic now lives inside a flow, connected through a trigger instead of a setting on the catalog item record.

Flow Designer's Service Catalog trigger fires on Requested Item Created, and it gets scoped to exactly one catalog item by filtering on the Requested Item's cat_item reference field. That scoping really matters. Without it, every single catalog request on every item in the entire catalog would fire this same flow. With it, a flow built to fulfill one specific software license item only ever runs for requests of that exact item, nothing else.

Once the trigger fires, the flow has the live Requested Item record available as a data pill, the same mechanism you learned back in Lesson 5. Buried inside that record are the catalog item's variables from Course 3: whatever the requester typed, picked, or selected gets stored against the Requested Item and exposed to the flow as a pill. A License Cost variable becomes a pill you can drag straight into an If/Else condition or a Create Record action, no re-typing required.

A single Request can contain several Requested Items at once, like someone ordering a laptop and a monitor in the same cart checkout. Triggering on the Request record would fire one flow execution covering every item together, with no clean way to isolate one item's fulfillment logic from another's. Triggering on the Requested Item instead gives each item its own independent flow execution, scoped to its own variables, even when it shares a Request with other items.

Take a real example: a 'New Software License Request' catalog item collects a License Cost variable and a Software Name variable. The flow's trigger condition is set to Requested Item Created where cat_item equals that exact item. The flow's first real step looks up the Requested Item's License Cost variable as a data pill, ready to feed the approval branching logic covered in the very next lesson.

So that's the real connection: catalog item to flow, made through a Requested Item trigger scoped by cat_item, carrying genuine variable data the moment it fires. Up next, we chain multiple approval stages together to handle requests that need more than one sign-off before they're fulfilled.
